## Report on `region_012` (region.fasta)

**Basic description.** One 3,000 bp DNA sequence, no ambiguous bases. Composition: A 25.9 %, C 28.0 %, G 26.1 %, T 20.0 % → **GC = 54.1 %**.

### 1. Compositional discontinuity (most obvious global feature)
The sequence is not compositionally uniform: it consists of an AT-rich block followed by a GC-rich block.

| Segment (1‑based) | Length | GC |
|---|---|---|
| 1–700 | 700 bp | **43.9 %** |
| 701–3000 | 2300 bp | **57.2 %** |

The change occurs around position ~700–790 (in 25‑bp windows GC goes from 0.36–0.52 in the first 700 bp to repeatedly 0.6–0.7 after). The shift roughly coincides with a gene boundary (below), which is the classic signature of a junction between DNA of different origin (e.g. a foreign/inserted segment in a host genome) rather than a smooth transition.

### 2. Long open reading frames
The sequence is definitely *not* random – it contains several stop-free reading frames far longer than composition-matched shuffled controls.

| ORF | Strand | Coordinates (1‑based, incl. stop) | Protein | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ORF1 | forward | **39–791** (ATG 39–41; TAA 789–791) | 250 aa | Hydrophilic (GRAVY −0.33); one C-terminal hydrophobic stretch ≈ residues 208–234 |
| ORF2 | reverse | **788–1744** (ATG = fwd 1742–1744; TAA = fwd 788–790) | 318 aa | Soluble; contains P-loop/ABC-type ATPase motifs (see below) |
| ORF3 | reverse | **1600–2592** (ATG = fwd 2590–2592; TGA = fwd 1600–1602) | 330 aa | Very hydrophobic (GRAVY +1.0), ~8–10 predicted transmembrane helices → integral membrane protein |

**ORF2 is the most convincing gene.** Its product carries the three diagnostic motifs of a P-loop (ABC-type) ATPase:
* Walker A / P-loop **GPNGCGKST** – residues 87–95 (reverse strand, fwd coords 2716–2742)
* ABC-family signature **LSGGQ** – residues 191–195 (fwd 2416–2430)
* Walker B **…AIMLLDEPTT…** – residues ~211–221 (fwd 2347–2358)

Motif spacing is canonical, so this is a genuine ABC-type ATPase rather than a chance ORF. Notably, ORF2 (ATPase) plus ORF3 (membrane protein) resemble the two subunit types of an ABC transporter, but here they are separate ORFs.

### 3. Gene arrangement
* **ORF1 (forward) and ORF2 (reverse) are convergent**: their stop codons lie only 3 bp apart (789–791 and 788–790), i.e. the two genes point at each other with essentially no intergenic space.
* **ORF2 and ORF3 lie on the same (reverse) strand and overlap over 1600–1744 (145 bp) in different reading frames.** Overlapping genes on one strand are possible but unusual over this length, so ORF3's status is less certain than ORF2's.

### 4. Statistical support
Mononucleotide-shuffled controls (500 replicates): the AT-rich half (1–800) never produced an ORF longer than ~183 codons, while ORF1 is 251 codons (p ≪ 0.002). Over the whole sequence the longest observed run (335 codons, the ORF2/ORF3 region) exceeded every shuffled replicate (max 312). So coding structure is real, though the individual long ORFs in the GC-rich half are less decisive because GC-rich DNA generates long ORFs by chance.

### 5. Negative results
No inverted repeats ≥ 20 bp (no hairpins/palindromes), no tandem/simple-sequence repeats, no common restriction sites, no σ70 −10/−35 or Shine–Dalgarno (AGGAGG) consensus at plausible positions, and no ambiguous bases.

**Summary.** The region is not featureless: it contains at least one clearly coding segment – a reverse-strand gene at 788–1744 encoding a P-loop/ABC-type ATPase – plus two further long ORFs (forward 39–791 and reverse 1600–2592, the latter a probable polytopic membrane protein), and it shows a marked AT-rich → GC-rich compositional shift near position 700. The gene-boundary/GC-shift coincidence and the overlapping/convergent ORF arrangement are the most unusual aspects.
